title: Osho on the Way of the Tao
description: What Osho taught about the Tao, in plain words. The old Taoists of China looked at water, at trees, at empty bowls, and learned how to live without fighting. Chuang Tzu's useless tree, Cook Ding and his knife that never went blunt, the empty hub of the wheel, the farmer who only said maybe, and the monkeys who were given three nuts in the morning. Then a meditation on letting go.

chapters.title: Osho on the Way of the Tao
chapters.ref: Osho, My Way: The Way of the White Clouds

beats.say: Two and a half thousand years ago, in China, an old man was leaving his country, riding on a buffalo. At the border, the guard stopped him and said: before you go, write down what you know.
That old man was Lao Tzu. And the little book he wrote that night became the Tao Te Ching. The Book of the Way.
The Tao cannot be explained. Lao Tzu says so on the very first page. But it can be lived. It is the way of water, the way of a tree, the way of things when you stop pushing them.
Osho gave many talks on Lao Tzu. His advice was: "Whatsoever you are, accept it so totally that nothing is left to be achieved." Tonight, let us walk a little way along the Way.
A carpenter and his student were travelling. They came upon an enormous old oak tree, so big that a thousand oxen could rest in its shade.

The student stood there in wonder. But the carpenter did not even stop. That tree is useless, he said. Its wood is soft. Make a boat, it sinks. Make a box, it rots. Nobody cuts it, because it is good for nothing.

That night the tree came to the carpenter in a dream. Useless? it said. The useful trees, the fruit trees, the straight trees, are cut down when they are young. Their branches are broken for their fruit.
I have worked for years to be useless. And because of it, I am alive. I have grown this big. Now even you can sit in my shade.
The society wants you to be useful. Useful to the factory, useful to the government, useful to your family's ambitions. And it will cut you to size for it.
Be useful, if you must. But keep something in you that is good for nothing. Something that only sings, only dances, only sits and watches the clouds.
Osho taught: not everything must be useful. That useless part of you is the most precious. It is the part that grows into a great tree.
Chuang Tzu tells of a cook named Ding, who worked in the kitchen of a prince. One day the prince watched him cutting up an ox.
And it was like a dance. His hand moved, his shoulder turned, his foot stepped, and the knife sang through the meat, as if keeping time to music.
The prince said: wonderful! What skill! And the cook put down his knife and said: it is not skill, my lord. It is the Tao.

When I began, all I could see was the ox. After three years, I no longer saw the whole ox. Now I don't look with my eyes at all. I feel the spaces between the joints, and the knife simply follows them.

An ordinary cook changes his knife every month, because he chops at the bone. A good cook changes it every year, because he cuts. I have had this knife for nineteen years, and it is as sharp as the day it was made.
The prince said: from my cook, I have learned how to live.
Osho taught: don't fight life, flow with it. The man who fights goes blunt. The man who feels the spaces moves through life without wearing out.
Lao Tzu says: The highest excellence is like that of water.
Look at water. It is soft. It never fights. Put a rock in its way, and it does not argue with the rock. It goes around.
It goes to the lowest place, the place everybody else avoids. It is not ambitious. It does not want to be on top.
And yet... drop by drop, it cuts through mountains. Give it time, and the hardest rock becomes sand.
We are taught to be hard. To push, to fight, to win. And we break. Water does not break, because it has no shape to defend.
Watch a river meeting a dam. It does not attack. It simply waits, and rises, and rises, patiently, until one day it flows over the top.
That is the strength of the soft. The tree that bends in the storm survives. The great hard tree that refuses to bend is the one that falls.
Osho taught: be like water. Soft, low, flowing... and unstoppable.
And another chapter: The thirty spokes unite in the one nave; but it is on the empty space that the use of the wheel depends.
Look at a cart wheel. Thirty spokes, all coming to the centre. And at the very centre... a hole. Nothing. And that nothing is what makes the wheel turn.
A clay pot is useful because it is empty inside. A room is useful because of the space between the walls. Fill the pot with stones, and you cannot carry water in it.
We fill our minds like this. With knowledge, opinions, worries, plans. There is no space left. And then we wonder why nothing new can come in.
Meditation is making space. Not adding one more thing. Taking things out, until there is a clean, open emptiness at the centre.
Osho taught: find the empty centre. From there, the whole wheel of your life can turn without effort.
An old farmer had one horse, and one day it ran away. The neighbours came and said: what bad luck! And the farmer said: maybe.
A week later the horse came back, and it brought seven wild horses with it. The neighbours said: what good luck! And the farmer said: maybe.
His son tried to ride one of the wild horses, was thrown off, and broke his leg. What bad luck! said the neighbours. Maybe, said the farmer.
Then soldiers came to the village to take all the young men away to the war. They saw the boy with his broken leg and left him behind. What good luck! said the neighbours.
And the farmer said... maybe.
We decide too quickly. This is good, this is bad. But life is much bigger than our little judgements. One event leads to another, and another, and the story is never finished.
Osho taught: don't divide life into good and bad. The farmer simply did not close the book after one page. The next time something happens, say: maybe. And watch.
A man who kept monkeys told them: from now on, you will get three chestnuts in the morning and four in the evening. The monkeys were furious. They screamed and jumped and shook the cages.
So the keeper said: all right. Four in the morning, and three in the evening. And the monkeys were delighted.
Seven chestnuts, the same seven chestnuts. Nothing had changed. Only the words had changed, and the monkeys were happy.
We laugh at the monkeys. But look at how we quarrel, in families, between religions, between nations, over three in the morning and four in the evening.
Osho loved Chuang Tzu's humour. The wise man, says Chuang Tzu, does not fight about names. He lets the monkeys have their way, and rests in the balance of heaven.
Now lie down, if you can, or sit, and let go, as Osho taught. Let the body become heavy. Close your eyes. Let the floor hold you.
Imagine you are floating on a slow river. You don't have to swim. The water holds you. The river knows the way to the sea.
Let go of the shoulders. Let go of the jaw. Let go of the hands. Let go of the little effort behind the eyes.
Thoughts come, like leaves floating past on the water. Let them float. Don't pick them up. Don't push them away.
You are not doing anything. Things are being done. The breath is breathing. The heart is beating. The river is flowing.
This is the Tao. Not something you achieve. Something you stop resisting.
Rest here, in the current. Soft, like water. Empty, like the hub of the wheel.
And slowly, let the river bring you back to the shore. Take a deep breath. Open your eyes. Walk softly today.
